Unit 7 - Regression Review

James Flynn

September 23, 2026

Linear Regression

  • Linear regression (OLS) is the workhorse behind the methods we use for causal inference
  • It can be used for
    • DiD
    • IV (at least partially)
    • RDD
    • We can often get causal estimates without these
  • Let’s refresh how it works

Regression Mechanics

Remember SST, SSR and SSE?

Total Sum of Squares (SST):

\(SST = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar{y})^2\)

Explained Sum of Squares (SSE):

\(SSE = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{y_i}-\bar{y})^2\)

Sum of Squared Residuals (SSR):

\(SSR = \sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{u}^2)\)

SST, SSR, SSE (cont’d)

\(SST = SSR + SSE\)

-Who remembers how to calculate \(R^2\)?

\(R^2\) formula

  • \(R^2\) is the ratio of total variation in y that is explained by our OLS line:

\(R^2 = \frac{SSE}{SST} = 1-\frac{SSR}{SST}\)

\(R^2 = 0 \implies\) no relationship

\(R^2 = 1 \implies\) perfect linear relationship

Don’t fixate too much on \(R^2\)

  • It can be a useful measure
    • However, it tells us nothing about causality
  • \(R^2\) more valuable for ML and prediction
    • Even then, it can be overutilized
    • Can also tell us how good our controls are
  • That said, we are going to fixate on \(R^2\) for a minute

Regression Mechanics (cont’d)

  • We’ll start with some definitions

  • Expected value - the expected value of a random variable is the sum of all possible values a variable can take multiplied by the probability of drawing that value

    • Also called the population mean or expectation

  • Suppose x can take values \(x_1, x_2,...,x_k\), each with probability \(f(x_1),f(x_2),...,f(x_k)\)

Expected Value Formula

\[E[X] = \sum_{n=1}^k x_nf(x_n)\]

  • Example - Dice Roll 1(1/6)+2(1/6)+3(1/6)+4(1/6)+5(1/6)+6(1/6) = 21/6 = 3.5

Example 2 - Mega Millions

  • On the day I wrote this slide, the Mega Millions jackpot was $33 million
  • Odds of winning: 1 in 302.6 million
  • Ticket costs $2
    • 0.00000033% chance of winning $32,999,998
    • 99.99999967% chance of losing $2
  • Expected value = .11 - 2 = -$1.89

  • Another example - expected goals in hockey/soccer

E[X] is a weighted mean

  • If observations have equal weight (probability), E[X] is just the mean
  • When would observations have unequal weight?
    • Dice roll with two die
    • Representative surveys

Introducing Variance using E[]

  • The variance of a random variable X is

\[V(X) = \sigma^2 = E[(X-E[X])^2]\]

  • The inside function measures raw deviation from the mean
  • The outside E[] averages the inside function

Properties of the Variance

  • \[V(\alpha X) = \alpha^2V(X) \]
  • \[V(X+\beta) = V(X) \]
  • \[V(constant) = 0 \]

Variance and Covariance

  • Variance measures the spread of one variable
  • Covariance measure how much two variables move together
  • Covariance formula:

\[ Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] \]

Class Exercise

Show that:

\[ Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] \]

in R using Goals and Assists from the NHL dataset

nhl <- haven::read_dta("NHL Master Dataset.dta") %>%
    filter(year>2012)

Solution

nhl <- nhl %>% mutate(goals_assists = Goals * Assists) 

E_goals_assists <- mean(nhl$goals_assists)
E_goals <- mean(nhl$Goals)
E_assists <- mean(nhl$Assists)

cov_goals_assists <- E_goals_assists - E_goals*E_assists
cov_goals_assists
## [1] 78.89663
cov(nhl$Goals,nhl$Assists)
## [1] 78.91159

Unpacking Covariance

  • Cov(X,Y) > 0 implies X and Y move together
  • Cov(X,Y) < 0 implies X and Y move in the opposite direction
  • Cov(X,Y) = 0 does not mean there is no relationship
    • Could be nonlinear relationship

Let’s go through some common regression hacks

Let’s use the NHL data to illustrate some common moves

nhl <- nhl %>% 
    mutate(Log_sal=log(Salary),log_points=log(Points)) %>%
    filter(is.na(Salary)==FALSE)

Why take logs?

Log transformation

  • When does it make sense to take logs?
  • Benefits
    • Linearizes data which takes extreme values
    • Reduces skew
    • Mitigates the effect of outliers
    • Can improve interpretability
  • Concerns
    • Can’t take log of 0 (why??)
    • Not appropriate for linear data
    • Can lead to overfitting

What to do with log(0) issue

  • Most common: log(x+1)
    • Get ready to fight
  • Take square root
    • Won’t help with negatives
  • Inverse hyperbolic sine transformation
    • Similar properties to log
    • sinh(x)
    Don’t just ignore it

Interpreting logs

  • level-level: change in x \(\implies\) change in y
  • log-level: change in x \(\implies\) % change in y
  • level-log: % change in x \(\implies\) change in y
  • log-log: % change in x \(\implies\) % change in y
    • What do we call this last one?

Polynomials of X variables

  • Often we’ll have a nonlinear relationship with one of our variables
  • Let’s look at how points per season depends on age
nhl <- nhl %>% mutate(age2 = Age^2)

Let’s take a look

m1 <- lm(Points ~ Age, data = nhl)
m2 <- lm(Points ~ Age + age2, data = nhl)
msummary(list(m1,m2), stars = TRUE, gof_omit = 'AIC|BIC|Lik|Adj.|F|R2|RMSE')

How to interpret polynomials

  • Need to take derivative wrt age

\[Points = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Age + \beta_2 Age^2\]

\[\frac{d Points}{dAge} = \beta_1 + 2\beta_2 Age \]

\[\equiv 2.493 - .036(Age)\]

Also known as…

  • When we include a dummy for each value of a variable, this is also called a ‘fixed effect’
  • Most commonly with time and geography
    • Year FE - controls for time-varying aspect of all groups
    • Unit FE (county?) - Controls for time-invariant characteristics of each area
  • Put them together for TWFE (what could go wrong?)

What about interaction terms?

Let’s pause and think about ‘controlling’ more

  • What does it mean to ‘control’ for X?
    • We will use the Frisch, Waugh, Lovell (FWL) theorem

FWL Setup

  • Beginning with our education-wages problem
  • Underlying ability is endogenous
  • What if we add SAT score to our regression?

\[wages = \beta_0 + \beta_1 ed\]

becomes

\[wages = \beta_0 + \beta_1 ed + \beta_2 SAT\] - \(\beta_1\) is interpreted as ‘the increase in wages from an additional year of schooling, holding SAT score constant’

What is held constant?

Our model is now:

\[E[wage|ed,SAT] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 ed + \beta_2 SAT\] so

\[\frac{\delta E[wage|ed,SAT]}{\delta ed} = \beta_1\]

  • Note that \(\beta_1\) is not a function of SAT

Instead of running the regression

  • Run two regressions \(X_2\) on the RHS
  • One with \(X_1\) as the DV, and one with \(Y\) as the DV.
  • Calculate residuals (denote as \(Y^*\) and \(X_1^*\))
  • Now estimate:

\[Y^* = X_1^*\gamma + u^*\] using normal OLS. Now:

\(\hat{\gamma} = \hat{\beta_1}\) and \(\hat{u^*}=\hat{u}\)

Let me prove it to you

SAT <- rnorm(10000)
ed <- rnorm(10000) + .2*SAT
wages <- runif(10000,10,100) + 2*ed + SAT

summary(lm(wages~SAT + ed))
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = wages ~ SAT + ed)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -45.349 -22.266  -0.323  22.415  45.292 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  54.9302     0.2584 212.596  < 2e-16 ***
## SAT           1.0807     0.2658   4.066 4.83e-05 ***
## ed            1.7769     0.2609   6.810 1.03e-11 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 25.84 on 9997 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.007491,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.007293 
## F-statistic: 37.73 on 2 and 9997 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

First step

res_1 <- lm(ed~SAT)$residuals
res_2 <- lm(wages~SAT)$residuals
FWL_reg <- lm(res_2 ~ res_1)
summary(FWL_reg)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = res_2 ~ res_1)

Class exercise

  • Prove this to yourself using any three variables
  • Can use the hockey data or any other data
    • Or you can make data up like I did

So what was the point of this?

  • What we did here was mechanically the exact same thing as including SAT in our regression
  • We first removed the effect of SAT on ed and wages (by residualizing)
  • Then we regressed the SAT-free part of ed on the SAT-free part of wages
  • This is how we should think about it anytime we include `controls’ in a regression

FWL informs each of the following

  • Interpret our coefficients
  • Understand when/how our regression is identified
    • What if SAT absorbed all the variation in ed?
  • See how controls affect the precision of \(\hat{\beta_1}\)

Last note about controls

  • Adding controls influences the SE of \(\beta_1\)
  • We will do a deep dive on standard errors next week, but:

\[SE(\beta_1) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_i \hat{u_i^*}^2}{\sum_i(x_i^*-\bar{x^*})^2}}\] - We can reduce SE (and our p-values) by including controls that soak up more variation in y than they do in x

Shifting towards causal thinking

  • We have two variables, X and Y
  • We want to know if X affects Y
  • Three key questions
    • Does anything else affect Y?
    • What is the functional form connecting X and Y
    • How to distinguish correlation from causation
  • We will use our more rigorous understanding of what ‘controlling’ does

As always, we start with a model

The linear bivariate regression model we know and love:

\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + u\]

  • This assumes a linear relationship
  • \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are pop. parameters
    • We never observe these
    • Our goal is to estimate them using data and assumptions

We have our OLS slope estimate

\(\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{cov(x,y)}{var(x)}\)

  • Can be computed whenever var(x) is not zero
    • This means we need variation in x
    • We can’t use a sample of all high school grads to get the returns to HS
  • With \(\hat{\beta_1}\), \(\hat{\beta_0}\) is straightforward to compute
  • Our residual, \(\hat{u}\), is therefore:

\(\hat{u_i} = y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1}x_i\)

Important to note difference between \(u\) and \(\hat{u}\)

  • \(u\) is unobservable
  • \(\hat{u}\) can always be calculated if we have \(\beta\)’s
  • residual represents the variation in y that is unexplained by our model
  • error term represents the variation in y that is random

Let’s think about how to interpret regressions

  • Keeping the \(E[]\) notation, \(\hat{\beta_1}\) tells us:

\(E[y|x] = \beta_0 + \beta_1x\)

  • Interpretation:

\[\beta_0 = E[y|x=0]\]

\[\beta_1 = \frac{dE[y|x]}{dx}\]

Interpretation - Multiple Regression

\(E[y|x,Z] = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \beta_2Z\)

  • Where Z is a vector of k controls
  • Now our interpretation of \(\beta_1\) is:

\[\beta_1 = \frac{dE[y|x,Z]}{dx}\]

  • \(\beta_1\) tells us the effect of x on y, after eliminating the effect of Z on both x and y

Checklist for running a causal regression

  • If I include these controls, is my parameter of interest identified
    • Is there enough variation to detect an effect?
  • If so, how?
  • Is the identifying variation plausibly as good as randomization?

Omitted Variable Bias (OVB)

  • If your variation is not as good as an experiment, often it is because you are missing some elements of \(X_i\) (some control)
  • Question: if a full regression model has a causal interpretation and we leave a variable out, what goes wrong?
    • Note: the idea of running the wrong regression only exists when answering a causal question. The conditional expectation interpretation is always valid.

OVB Formula

  • Suppose the true model of earnings and education was:

\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 ed_i + \beta_2 SAT_i + u_i\]

  • But instead you only run:

\[y_i = b_0 + b_1 ed_i + \epsilon_i\]

  • What is \(\hat{b_1}\) an estimate of?

OVB formula (cont’d)

\[b_1 = \frac{cov(ed,y)}{var(ed)}\]

\[\equiv \frac{cov(ed, \beta_0 + \beta_1 ed_i + \beta_2 SAT_i + u_i)}{var(ed)}\]

\[\equiv \frac{\beta_1 var(ed) + \beta_2 cov(ed, SAT)}{var(ed)}\]

\[\equiv \beta_1 + \beta_2\frac{cov(ed,SAT)}{var(ed)}\]

OVB formula (cont’d)

  • Bias is simply \(\beta_2\frac{cov(ed,SAT)}{var(ed)}\)

  • Note that this is \(\beta_2 \delta_1\) with \(\delta_1\) from

\[ SAT_i = \delta_0 + \delta_1 ed_i + residual\]

  • Bias is \(\beta_2 \delta_1\)
    • or the effect of SAT on wage, scaled by the relationship between SAT and ed

When is this not a problem?

  • Need \(\beta_2 \delta_1 = 0\)
    • Either SAT does not affect wage
    • or SAT and ed uncorrelated
  • If either of these is true, this is not an omitted variable

If we don’t have the OVB, we can still likely sign the bias

Class exercise

  • Using NHL data, let’s find out if games played (GP) is an omitted variable in the regression:

\[\text{Log_sal}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Goals_i + u_i\]

  • First, sign the bias using the table in the previous slide
  • Then, use the formula \(OVB = \beta_2 \delta_1\) to calculate it
  • Finally, run the regression with and without GP
    • Was our calculation right? How can you tell?

Answers

  • First, sign the bias
    • We’d expect the coefficient on GP to be positive in explaining log_sal (+)
    • Also expect correlation between GP and Goals to be positive (+)
    • OVB should be positive

Sign the bias

#beta_2
lm1 <- lm(Log_sal~Goals+GP,data=nhl)
beta_2 <- summary(lm1)$coefficients[3,1]
beta_2
## [1] 0.009513985
cor_goals_gp <- cor(nhl$Goals, nhl$GP)
cor_goals_gp
## [1] 0.6371922
beta_2 >0 & cor_goals_gp >0
## [1] TRUE

Calculate the bias

  • We have \(\beta_2\), just need \(\delta_1\)
#delta_1
lm2 <- lm(GP~Goals,data=nhl)
delta_1 <- summary(lm2)$coefficients[2,1]
delta_1
## [1] 2.169138

Now multiply

OVB <- beta_2 * delta_1
OVB
## [1] 0.02063715

Let’s see what it does in our regression

m1 <- lm(Log_sal ~ Goals, data = nhl)
m2 <- lm(Log_sal ~ Goals + GP, data = nhl)
msummary(list(m1,m2), stars = TRUE, gof_omit = 'AIC|BIC|Lik|Adj.|F')

+ p < 0.1, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001

(0.013) (0.018)
Goals 0.052*** 0.031***
(0.001) (0.001)
GP 0.010***
